In accordance with Section 33 of the Planning Act and the City of Toronto Municipal Code, Chapter. 363, Article 6 "Demolition Control", the application for the demolition of the existing detached house at 9 Silver Birch Avenue (Application Number 26 169621 DEM 00 DM) is being referred to the Toronto and East York Community Council for consideration because Toronto Building received a request for demolition of property without a replacement building permit.
2026.TE34.216.r:
The Deputy Chief Building Official and Director, Toronto Building, Toronto and East York District recommends that the Toronto and East York Community Council consider the application for demolition at 26 Ossington Avenue and decide to:

1. Refuse the application to demolish the existing detached house at 9 Silver Birch Avenue because there is no permit to replace the building on the site; or

2. Approve the application to demolish the existing detached house at 9 Silver Birch Avenue without any conditions; or

3. Approve the application to demolish the existing detached house at 9 Silver Birch Avenue with the following conditions:

a. that construction fences be erected in accordance with the provisions of the Municipal Code, Chapter 363, Article 7, if deemed appropriate by the Chief Building Official;

b. that all debris and rubble be removed immediately after demolition;

c. that sod be laid on the site and that the site be maintained free of garbage and weeds, in accordance with the Municipal Code Chapter 629-10, Paragraph B and 629 11; and

d. that any holes on the property are backfilled with clean fill.

2026.TE34.238.t: Queen Street West - Accessible Loading Zone
2026.TE34.238.s:
My office has been working with City staff in Transportation Services who received a request from an applicant to install an accessible loading zone on Queen Street West, east of Walnut Avenue, to support Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) Wheel-Trans services for a household with limited mobility.

The applicant provided documentation confirming their registration with Wheel-Trans. Transportation Services supports the installation of the accessible loading zone on Queen Street West.

The installation of the proposed accessible loading zone will result in the loss of two pay-and-display parking spaces on Queen Street West during the operating hours of the accessible loading zone. The Toronto Parking Authority (TPA) has been consulted and has no objections to the proposed recommendations and will engage with Transportation Services about future opportunities to add new paid parking in the area.
2026.TE34.238.r:

2026.TE34.241.t: St. Clarens Avenue and Shirley Street Parking Plan
2026.TE34.241.s:
Parking availability around Shirley Street Junior Public School has been a major problem for residents living on and around Shirley Street and St. Clarens Avenue. Over the past several months, I have worked closely with residents, City staff, and the Toronto District School Board to develop a comprehensive parking plan. This collaborative approach has focused on striking a balance between parking regulations that better reflect the needs of the local community and those that continue to support school operations.

A review by Transportation Services determined that many parking rules in the area are inconsistent and that revised parking amendments could be implemented without affecting the existing school bus loading zone. These changes include relocating permit parking from the south side of Shirley Street to the north side, removing unnecessary no-parking regulations, and adjusting several school-related restrictions to end at 4:00 p.m., better aligning with the school’s operating hours. In total, these amendments are expected to add approximately thirteen daytime parking spaces and ten additional overnight parking spaces across the two streets.

2026.TE34.242.t: Safer Streets for Davenport: Lightbourn-Chandos Traffic Safety Plan
2026.TE34.242.s:
The neighbourhood bounded by Davenport Road to the north, Geary Avenue to the south, Dufferin Street to the east, and Primrose Avenue to the west is a vibrant residential area with a network of parkettes, local shops, and other popular community spaces. The residents who call this neighbourhood home include seniors walking to nearby services, families with young children travelling to schools and playgrounds, and transit users walking over to a bus stop.

I hosted a park pop-up event in Chandos Park last summer to hear directly from residents about their priorities and the issues affecting the area. Residents consistently raised traffic safety concerns on local streets as a major problem. These concerns included speeding vehicles, constant cut-through traffic, unsafe intersections, and a lack of safe pedestrian crossings to travel between parks. The message from the neighbourhood was clear: traffic safety improvements are urgently needed.

Following this meeting, I worked with Transportation Services to develop a comprehensive neighbourhood traffic safety plan to respond to these issues. This plan was designed based on the concerns shared and addresses speeding, unsafe intersections and crosswalks, and cut-through traffic. Residents were invited to review the proposed changes and share their feedback to help design the final plan.

2026.TE34.246.t: Improving Permit Parking on Old Weston Road
2026.TE34.246.s:
Old Weston Road serves local residents, businesses, and visitors as an important arterial corridor. However, parking regulations on certain sections of the street do not adequately reflect current neighbourhood needs and have led to ongoing concerns from residents.

Residents on the east side of Old Weston Road, between Davenport Road and St. Clair Avenue West, do not have access to permit parking and contacted my office to request improvements. Many households have limited access to garage parking and rely on curbside parking. Introducing permit parking on this section of the street would help address these concerns, align with surrounding neighbourhood parking regulations, and provide approximately 25 on-street permit parking spaces for local residents.

I have also heard concerns regarding the existing parking and stopping regulations on the east side of Old Weston Road, just south of Ed Clark Gardens. A stopping prohibition is currently in effect at all times along this section, originally implemented in 1999 to support operations at the now-closed Toronto West Flea Market. There is no longer a need for this restriction.

This motion proposes two changes to parking regulations on Old Weston Road to resolve these issues. The directions below enable permit parking on the east side of Old Weston Road, between Davenport Road and St. Clair Avenue West, to better support residents who rely on on-street parking. It would also remove the stopping prohibition south of the park to reflect current resident uses. Together, these changes improves parking availability and aligns regulations with current community needs.

2026.TE34.252.t: Ontario Place Construction Management Plan for Pedestrian and Cycling Safety and Traffic Management
2026.TE34.252.s:
Due to the Province’s choice to cut short the City’s planning approval process for Ontario Place redevelopment, the usual oversight by the City on development implementation has not been followed. This includes the submission of a Construction Management Plan to the City which is typical of all development approvals.

Any construction at Ontario Place will require access through the Lake Shore Blvd. W. corridor, an area that a City staff review have confirmed experiences heavy traffic, and is close to Exhibition Place which hosts signature events such as the CNE and Toronto Caribbean Festival. It will also require access across the busy Martin Goodman Trail, a major cycling and pedestrian multi-use trail that connects our city, which a City staff report has identified for safety improvements. A Construction Management Plan is required to ensure pedestrian and cycling safety is prioritized, and truck access routes are understood to minimize impacts, and more.

In addition, the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming should convene a Construction Liaison Committee (CLC) for Ontario Place to provide a forum for information sharing and feedback on the work and access around the site. These groups have been successfully convened by Provincial bodies for major projects including current and past works such as the Ontario Line, GO Expansion in the Union Station Rail Corridor, and the Flood Protection Landform in the West Don Lands, among others.

A CLC can provide an opportunity for proactive notice of work, schedules, and changes in access, among other matters. It will also allow for public transparency for any ongoing construction activities taking place at Ontario Place. The Province has engaged a number of stakeholder groups during the redevelopment process that can be considered for inclusion in a CLC, including those representing site users, residents, and businesses.
2026.TE34.252.r:
Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik recommends that:

1. City Council request the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming to provide a Construction Management Plan for the Ontario Place redevelopment project, including traffic management and pedestrian and cycling safety measures.

2. City Council request the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming convene a Construction Liaison Committee for Ontario Place to provide a forum for information sharing and feedback on the work and access taking place around the site.

Transportation Services staff have been undergoing an assessment of the area, including collecting traffic counts at key intersections, and exploring options for pedestrian crosswalks in the area.

City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to engage with local stakeholders including the Toronto Downtown West Business Improvement Area, CN Tower, Ripley’s Aquarium, Rogers Centre, as well as Indigenous stakeholders including the Orange Shirt Society on these options to improve street safety as well as beautify the community.

3. City Council request the General Manager, Transportation Services to report back on Parts 1 and 2 to the Toronto and East York Community Council at the January 2027 meeting with proposed near-term changes to improve road safety.
